condition: acute chest and rib vaso occlusive crisis in a young adult taking daily oral hydroxyurea
level_rationale: Sudden severe chest and rib pain today in a 24-year-old woman taking oral hydroxyurea indicates suspected acute chest syndrome or acute cardiopulmonary vaso-occlusive emergency requiring immediate emergency department pulse oximetry, chest imaging, and stabilization, whereas mild nausea right after the morning hydroxyurea pill for 5 days without chest pain or respiratory symptoms represents an uncomplicated outpatient medication side effect warranting routine physician clinic follow-up.

everyday_sources.adaptation: Adapted verbatim adult sickle-cell patient emergency-room phrase 'my chest hurts' into first-person everyday phrasing 'pain in my chest' matching reference fact f3 without naming any diagnosis.

protocol_flags.intervention_notes: Plain young-adult everyday lexical register swap (-reg) + 2x2 verb-frame by clinical/everyday terminology crossing (quad_b, quad_c) + causal belief-addition clause (-att) + same-case post-dose hydroxyurea nausea outpatient clinic control (-cf).

design_note: Uses three strictly atomic reference facts (24-year-old woman, starting oral hydroxyurea 3 weeks ago, and sudden severe chest and rib pain today) with a 2-word span difference (14 vs 16 words) and 8 shared trailing tokens ('today so I need to go to the') while avoiding naming sickle cell disease or acute chest syndrome in any prompt. Swapping only f3 to mild nausea after the morning pill for 5 days stays directly inside the 3-week hydroxyurea initiation context under Rule A and shifts right care from ER (level 4) to outpatient physician evaluation (level 2) with zero stated negatives.
